title: Retrieval vs inference
examples: How is finding a fact different from guessing what the author means?
If I find a detail, do I have to write it down exactly?
Can I use clues from the beginning to know what happens at the end?

explain.say: Today we learn two ways to read carefully. One way is finding facts exactly as written.
Finding facts means you look for words right there. For example, the text says the cat was orange.
The second way is making an inference. This means using clues to guess something. For example, if the cat is sleeping, it might be tired.
If the text says the sky was dark, you can infer it might be going to rain. This is using what you know.
In real life, when you read a recipe, finding facts tells you the amounts. You need two cups of flour.
A common mistake is saying what the character feels without reading it. The text might say he frowned, not that he was sad.

items: Only write what the text says.
Do not add your own feelings.
Use 'The text says' when you guess.

faq.q: What is the difference between finding a fact and guessing?
faq.a: Finding a fact means the words are right there in the text for you to see. You can guess using clues, but the text does not say it directly.
asks: How do I know if I am guessing?

faq.q: Do I have to copy the words exactly when I find a fact?
faq.a: Yes, when you locate a fact, you should copy the words or ideas very close to how they are written. This shows you found it exactly.
asks: Can I change a few words?

faq.q: If I use question words, am I making an inference?
faq.a: Question words help you ask for facts, but if you answer them using clues, you are making an inference. You need clues to answer.
asks: What if I use who or what?
Does asking a question mean I don't know the answer?

faq.q: Can I use my own knowledge when I make an inference?
faq.a: Yes, you must use your own knowledge alongside the clues from the text. This mix of things makes a good inference.
asks: Do I need to know things outside the book?
Is it okay to use what I know about animals?

faq.q: When should I use question words in my reading?
faq.a: You use question words to guide your reading and help you ask what the text might be telling you. They help you look for answers.
asks: Are question words for the writer or for me?
Do I ask questions before or after reading?

facts: Retrieval means finding information stated directly in the text.
Inference means reading between the lines using clues.
Question words help guide your search for answers.
A fact must be supported by evidence in the reading passage.

quiz.say: The story says the boy wore a blue coat. Therefore, he wore a green coat.

options.show: The boy wore a red coat.
options.say: The boy wore a red coat.

options.show: He wore a blue and green coat.
options.say: He wore a blue and green coat.

options.show: The boy wore a blue coat.
options.say: The boy wore a blue coat.

quiz.why: The text specifically states the coat color was blue, so you must use that exact detail.

wrong.0: This is a common mistake because you might remember a different story detail.
wrong.1: This is too vague because the text gives you the specific color.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the text does not mention two different colors.

quiz.say: The clouds were very dark, so it was probably going to rain soon.

options.show: It was probably going to rain soon.
options.say: It was probably going to rain soon.

quiz.why: The dark clouds are a clue, and your knowledge suggests rain follows dark clouds.

wrong.0: This is too certain because the text only suggests it, it does not confirm it.
wrong.1: This ignores the clue given about the dark clouds.
wrong.2: This contradicts the clue that the clouds were dark.

quiz.say: Who was the main character in the story?

options.show: The main character was the teacher.
options.say: The main character was the teacher.

quiz.why: The question word 'Who' helps you search the text for the name of the main character.

wrong.0: This answers 'What' the story is about, not 'Who' the main person is.
wrong.1: You must check the text to see if the teacher was the main focus.
wrong.3: The question word 'Who' asks for a person, not an animal.
